config.text: A sealed tomb in the Valley of the Kings.
A warning, it is said, guarded its door: death would come swiftly to anyone who disturbed the king.
And within five months of the tomb's opening, the man who had paid for the search was dead.
This is the curse of Tutankhamun, as it has been told for a hundred years.

So where did the curse come from?
In this episode, we follow the story from a step in the sand, to the newspapers of 1923, and back to tales of mummies written long before the tomb was found.
On the fourth of November, 1922, Egyptian workmen digging for the archaeologist Howard Carter uncovered a step cut into the rock, in the Valley of the Kings, near Luxor.
Carter had the stairway covered again, and sent a telegram to his patron in England, Lord Carnarvon.

config.text: On the twenty-sixth of November, with Carnarvon beside him, Carter made a small hole in a sealed doorway and held up a candle.

config.text: Asked if he could see anything, he answered, as he later wrote in his book: "Yes, wonderful things."
It was the tomb of a young king who had ruled more than three thousand years earlier.
Robbers had entered it in ancient times, but many of the things buried with him were still there.
On the sixteenth of February, 1923, before invited guests, the sealed door of the burial chamber was opened.
The discovery made headlines around the world.
Lord Carnarvon placed the reporting of the excavation in the hands of one London newspaper, The Times.

config.text: In the race for news, stories from outside the tomb began to fill the papers too.
In March 1923, Carnarvon fell ill with an infection, and then pneumonia.

config.text: On the fifth of April, he died in Cairo, at the age of fifty-six.
Newspapers around the world linked his death to the tomb.
They also reported the novelist Marie Corelli's belief in ancient powers protecting the tomb.
The writer Arthur Conan Doyle was quoted as suggesting that a spirit-like force guarding the tomb might be to blame.
On the same pages, other experts disagreed.
The famous warning appeared as the story was retold.
We have not found a reliable source placing those words in the tomb itself.
Among the tomb's real texts are wishes for the king's eternal life.
One alabaster cup carries a wish for him to live for millions of years.
Stories of mummies and the dangers of their tombs were already being read long before the discovery.
In eighteen sixty-nine, Louisa May Alcott, the author of Little Women, published "Lost in a Pyramid; or, The Mummy's Curse," a tale of seeds taken from a tomb that bring misfortune.

config.text: In eighteen ninety-two, Conan Doyle himself published "Lot number two forty-nine," in which a mummy is brought back to life.
Ancient Egypt did have warnings of its own.
One tomb chapel from around twenty-four hundred B C, more than a thousand years before Tutankhamun, warns that anyone who enters it unclean and does it harm will be judged by the great god.

The story grew around older tales of mummies, a sudden and tragic death, and arguments in the newspapers.
